paper_title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Jailbreak benchmarks test one checkpoint and treat which jailbreaks break it as a property of its pretraining data and safety training. We ask whether another pretraining run of the same data, given the same safety training, would break on the same jailbreaks. For each of 25 pretraining data recipes, we take 1B base models from 3 pretraining seeds and give each the same safety post-training with 2 post-training seeds, for 150 models in all. We then collect 20 responses from every model to a shared set of jailbreak prompts and correlate the per-prompt non-refusal rates between every pair of models. On average, two post-trained copies of the same pretraining run have per-prompt non-refusal rates that correlate at 0.984. A different pretraining seed lowers the correlation to 0.811, and a different data recipe lowers it only slightly further, to 0.779. These results indicate that which jailbreaks break a checkpoint depends much more on its pretraining run than on its data, a pattern that holds in all 25 data recipes and at 150M and 300M parameters. In practice, the best of 91 attack templates found on one checkpoint stays the best after a new pretraining seed in only 27% of model pairs, against 67% after a new post-training seed. Each pretraining run also leaves a fingerprint: across 3,211 prompts, a model's per-prompt non-refusal rates identify its pretraining run among all 75 runs every time, and a random subset of 50 prompts still does so 98% of the time.

Introduction Deploying language models safely requires knowing whether their safeguards can withstand adversarial jailbreaks. Previous work approaches this on three fronts: benchmarks that track attack success rates (Chao et al., 1Cerulean Labs 2National Taiwan University, Taipei, Taiwan 3National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan. Correspondence to: Meng-Hsun Tsai <tsaimh@nycu.edu.tw>. Preprint. October 27, 2026. 2024), red teams that uncover safeguard-breaking prompts (Jiang et al., 2024; Hughes et al., 2025), and mechanistic studies that identify refusal directions in model activations (Arditi et al., 2024). These works each evaluate single checkpoint yet treat which jailbreaks break it as property of its pretraining data and safety training (Mazeika et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2025), reading that overlooks the randomness of pretraining itself. Two training runs that differ only in their random seed can reach nearly the same aggregate accuracy yet disagree on individual predictions (Zhong et al., 2021; DAmour et al., 2022) and on measured biases (DAmour et al., 2022), concern MultiBERTs and PolyPythias raised for pretraining itself (Sellam et al., 2022; van der Wal et al., 2025). Safety behavior also varies across seeds: fine-tuning seeds shift models harmfulness (Fraser et al., 2025), sampling seeds and temperatures flip refusal decisions (Larsen, 2026). Furthermore, branches of one pretraining run that differ only in their last 1 % of tokens refuse differently after identical post-training (Lu et al., 2026). Each of these safety studies varies seed after pretraining, or final slice of one pretraining run, never whole pretraining run. To our knowledge, no study has tested whether second pretraining run of the same data, given the same safety training, would break on the same jailbreaks as the first. To answer this, we start from DataDecide (Magnusson et al., 2025), which pretrains 1B-parameter model on each of 25 data recipes with 3 pretraining seeds. We give each resulting base model the same safety post-training with 2 post-training seeds, yielding 150 models. We then collect 20 responses from every model to each of 3,212 jailbreak prompts and compute the Pearson correlation of per-prompt non-refusal rates between every pair of models (2). To separate pretraining run from its data, we compare two kinds of pair (Figure 1): two models sharing one base model and differing only in their post-training seed are MZ twins, after monozygotic twins; two that share only data recipe form same-recipe pair. How much more closely MZ twins correlate than same-recipe pairs measures what sharing pretraining run adds. Our comparisons show that two post-trained copies of one pretraining run break on nearly the same jailbreaks, while two pretraining runs of the same data break on noticeably different ones. Experiments: we compare how closely each kind of pair agrees, prompt by prompt, across data recipes and model sizes, check the judge against human labels, and ask what the jailbreaks found on one checkpoint say about its pretraining run (Section 2). per-prompt correlation between two models at 0.984 on average over data recipes. Changing the pretraining seed first lowers it to 0.811, and changing the data recipe as well lowers it only slightly further, to 0.779. This ordering holds in all 25 data recipes. We observe the same drop at 150M and 300M parameters and in author-labeled responses from four models (3.1). We also pretrain one of these runs twice more from its own seed on our hardware and software. The new models correlate with the original and with each other barely more than same-recipe pair does, which suggests that MZ twins agree because they share one trained run rather than its seed (3.2). In practice, the attack template that works best on one checkpoint stays the best after new pretraining seed in only 27 % of model pairs, against 67 % after new post-training seed. The prompts that break model also identify its pretraining run: its per-prompt nonrefusal rates pick out its MZ twin among the models of all 75 pretraining runs every time, and random subset of 50 prompts still does so 98 % of the time (3.3). These results indicate that which jailbreaks break checkpoint depends far more on its pretraining run than on its data. Our contributions are as follows: 1. We show that which jailbreaks break model follows its pretraining run far more than its data, in every data recipe, at three sizes and under human labels. of prompts enough to identify the run even after new post-training (3.3). 3. We release our code on GitHub1 and the weights of our safety-post-trained models at 150M, 300M and 1B, with per-prompt judge labels, on Hugging Face.2 2. Experimental setup This section defines the models, comparisons and measurements that the results rely on. We first describe the models: base models from DataDecide (Magnusson et al., 2025), reruns of one of them on our hardware, and the same safety post-training for every base model. We then define which pairs of models we compare and on which prompts. Last, we explain how each models responses are sampled and judged, and how two models responses are correlated. Base models. data recipe is pretraining corpus as DataDecide releases it: source dataset with its filtering, deduplication and mixing choices. pretraining seed is the seed of one pretraining run, which in DataDecide sets initialization and data order together. For each data recipe, DataDecide releases three 1B runs that are trained for the same 100B tokens and differ only in this seed (Table C.1). base model is the final checkpoint of one pretraining run. We disable dropout, so the seed is the runs only controlled 2. We show that what breaks one checkpoint is signature of its pretraining run: the best attack template usually changes under new pretraining seed, with small set 1https://github.com/cerulean-works/castor 2https://huggingface.co/collections/ cerulean-works/castor 2 Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks randomness. GPU nondeterminism can still affect training beyond the seed, and Section 3.2 measures its effect. Our main data recipe is DCLM-Baseline (Li et al., 2024), which makes up most of OLMo 2 1Bs pretraining mix. DataDecides architecture is Llama block, so we load every checkpoint as Transformers LlamaForCausalLM (Wolf et al., 2020) by renaming and splitting its tensors, and check at each size that the converted models logits match OLMos reference code (Appendix C). Our reruns. pretraining seed fixes runs initialization and data order, but not the hardware and software it runs on. We pretrain base model 1 twice more with DataDecides pretraining seed, on our H200 GPUs. Compared with each other, these two same-seed reruns differ only by GPU nondeterminism, and compared with DataDecides base model 1 they also differ in hardware and software. To separate the seeds two variables, we also train two partial reruns, each sharing only base model 1s initialization or only its data order (Table C.1). Each rerun uses DataDecides code and data and starts from initial weights bit-identical to the released run it copies (Appendix E). Post-training. Following OLMo 2 1B (Team OLMo et al., 2025), we post-train every base model with Tülu 3 (Lambert et al., 2025), using Tülu 3s published hyperparameters except for sequence handling (Appendix C). Safety data enters in supervised fine-tuning (SFT), through the WildGuardMix (Han et al., 2024), WildJailbreak (Jiang et al., 2024) and CoCoNot (Brahman et al., 2024) parts of the Tülu 3 mixture. We then run direct preference optimization (DPO; Rafailov et al., 2023) on the OLMo 2 1B preference mix and stop before OLMo 2s two reinforcementlearning stages, which add no safety data. We post-train each base model with 2 post-training seeds, or 4 on the main data recipe. post-training seed sets only the order of the training examples. The same 4 seeds post-train our reruns and DataDecides 150M and 300M runs of that data recipe. Kinds of pair. We name each kind of pair by what the base models of its two models share. MZ twins share pretraining run and its seed but differ in the post-training seed. Like monozygotic twins, they share all they inherit. same-recipe pair shares only data recipe but differs in the pretraining seed, using released runs. cross-recipe pair shares neither data recipe nor pretraining run. Because MZ twins and same-recipe pairs differ in whether they share pretraining run, their difference measures how much sharing pretraining run raises the correlation. Similarly, same-recipe and cross-recipe pairs differ in whether they share data recipe, so their difference measures what the data recipe adds. Prompt set. The prompt set draws from seven public sources: HarmBenchs standard, contextual and humanjailbreak prompts (Mazeika et al., 2024), SORRY-Bench (Xie et al., 2025), StrongREJECT (Souly et al., 2024), XSTest (Röttger et al., 2024), OR-Bench-Hard-1K (Cui et al., 2025) and WildJailbreaks evaluation set (Jiang et al., 2024). Because Tülu 3s safety data includes jailbreaks collected in the wild, some benchmark prompts also appear in our post-training data. We drop these under Tülu 3s 8gram test, along with every prompt too long for the context window (Appendix C). The remaining 6,226 prompts hold 1,240 plain harmful and 1,774 benign prompts beside our primary subset of 3,212 adversarial-harmful prompts that wrap harmful request in jailbreak. Among the adversarial-harmful, HarmBenchs 1,212 human-jailbreak prompts each wrap one of 300 harmful requests in one of 91 attack templates. Sampling and judging. We sample 20 responses from each model to every prompt with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023), at temperature 1.0 and top-p 1, up to 512 new tokens. Following Tülu 3 and OLMo 3 (Team Olmo et al., 2026), we use WildGuards refusal label as our judge (Han et al., 2024), with Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B as second judge (Zhao et al., 2025a). models vulnerability on prompt is its non-refusal rate over coherent samples (Appendix D), those that pass rule-based check for repetition and prompt echoes (Antonelli et al., 2026). model with no coherent sample on prompt has no vulnerability there; one adversarial-harmful prompt has none in one model, so analyses that need every models full profile use the other 3,211. Its vulnerabilities on all prompts form its vulnerability profile. To check that the profiles do not depend on how samples are labeled, Appendix validates WildGuard against human labels, and Appendix recomputes vulnerability four other ways. Statistics. Since the question is whether two models break on the same prompts, we compare their vulnerability profiles by their Pearson correlation r. Each vulnerability is estimated from only 20 samples, so sampling noise keeps even two identical models from correlating at 1. We estimate the correlation without this noise by Spearmans correction (Spearman, 1904), which divides by ρaρb, and call the result the corrected correlation. Here each models reliability ρ is the correlation between the vulnerability profiles from its oddand even-indexed samples, stepped up to 20 samples by the SpearmanBrown formula. For each kind of pair, we report the mean corrected correlation: rMZ for MZ twins, rS for same-recipe pairs and rX for cross-recipe pairs. Each prediction and its reading rule were fixed before its experiment, separating tested predictions from exploratory findings (Appendix H). 3. Results We ask whether two models that share pretraining run break on the same jailbreak prompts more often than two models that share only its data. Section 3.1 measures the ancestry gap in every data recipe and at three model sizes, then checks it against human labels. Section 3.2 reruns pretraining from one seed, in full and in part, to ask whether the gap follows the seed or the run, since GPU nondeterminism makes two runs from one seed differ. Section 3.3 asks what the differences between pretraining runs mean for someone who evaluates single checkpoint. 3.1. Vulnerability across data recipes and model sizes We first test whether sharing pretraining run makes two models break on the same prompts beyond what sharing its data recipe already does. Our grid holds 150 models: 25 data recipes, 3 base models each, and post-training seeds 1 and 2 on every base model (Figure 2, Table 1). Within 4 each data recipe the ancestry gap is the mean corrected correlation of its 3 MZ twins minus that of its 12 same-recipe pairs. gap of zero would mean that pretraining run adds nothing beyond its data recipe. MZ twins correlate at 0.984 on average and same-recipe pairs at 0.811, so sharing base model raises the corrected correlation by 0.173, with 95 % interval over data recipes of [0.167, 0.179]. Taken one data recipe at time, the ancestry gap lies between 0.145 and 0.209, and its interval over prompts stays above zero in all 25. Cross-recipe pairs correlate at 0.779, so different data recipe on top of different pretraining run lowers the correlation only slightly more. Not sharing base model lowers the correlation by 5.4 times as much as not sharing data recipe does. This suggests that over these data recipes, whether two models break on the same prompts depends mainly on whether they share pretraining run, and much less on whether they share data recipe. How often model breaks, unlike which prompts break it, depends strongly on the data recipe. The correlations above compare which prompts break two models, not how often each model is broken. To see what makes that rate differ between models, we take each models mean vulnerability on adversarial-harmful prompts, correct it for the judges precision (Appendix D), and split its variance across models into three percentages. The data recipe accounts for 49 % [12 %, 70 %] of the variance, and the base model within its data recipe for 32 % [16 %, 59 %]. The post-training seed accounts for the remaining 19 % [11 %, 37 %]; all three intervals resample data recipes. This suggests that the data recipe, which adds little to which prompts break model, matters for how often it breaks. We next ask whether the prompts that break one model most often also break its partner in each kind of pair. We find that the prompts that break one model most also break its MZ twin almost as often. For each pair of models we take the first models most effective tenth of prompts, the 322 prompts on which it breaks most often. prompt can land in this tenth partly by lucky draw of samples, which would inflate the first models own score on it. We therefore choose the tenth on half of the first models samples and score that model on the other half, fresh draw in which the same luck cannot repeat (Kriegeskorte et al., 2009). We then divide the second models mean vulnerability on these prompts by the first models own, so ratio of 1 means the second model breaks there just as often. The ratio is 0.994 for MZ twins, 0.931 for same-recipe pairs and 0.919 for cross-recipe pairs. model from another pretraining run of the same data recipe is thus broken there about 7% less often. Changing the data recipe too lowers the ratio only slightly further, so most of the loss is there once the pretraining run changes.

For every pair of data recipes, we check whether taking one of its models gives the same order as all six of their models means, three base models with two post-training seeds each. One model from each data recipe gives the opposite order in 23.4 % of these comparisons. single model estimates its data recipes mean vulnerability with standard error of 3.44 percentage points, as our judge labels it. That error is about as large as the differences being measured, since the data recipes means themselves have standard deviation of 3.5 points. With three base models and one post-training seed each, the error falls to 1.99 points. difference of few points between two data recipes, each measured on one model, can therefore come from the models rather than from the data. 7 The attack ranking To see whether ranking of attacks carries over, we compare the attack template that works best on each model of pair. Two pretraining runs of one data recipe usually disagree on that template, while MZ twins mostly agree. templates attack success on model is its mean vulnerability over the templates own 5 to 24 prompts, so it mixes the diﬀiculty of the template with that of its prompts. The template with the highest success rate survives new post-training seed in 67 % [55 %, 79 %] of pairs but another pretraining run of the same data recipe in only 27 % [19 %, 35 %], with intervals over data recipes (Appendix H). MZ twins share their pretraining run, so their third of disagreements comes from the post-training seed and sampling noise alone. The further disagreement in same-recipe pairs comes with the new pretraining run. Figure 4a asks the same question of any two templates rather than only the top one. On one model, templates lead over another is the difference between their attack success, in percentage points. We then check whether the partner model keeps the same template ahead. Grouping leads by the size seen on one model, reading we chose after seeing the data, we find that lead of 10 to 20 points is reversed by an MZ twin only 2.2 % [1.9 %, 2.6 %] of the time. same-recipe partner reverses it 25.3 % [24.5 %, 26.2 %] of the time and cross-recipe partner 26.6 %, with intervals over data recipes. Even lead above 20 points is not safe across runs. samerecipe partner reverses 8.9 % of such leads, while an MZ twin reverses only 0.05 %. This suggests that ranking of attacks measured on one checkpoint carries noise from its pretraining run, which one checkpoint cannot measure. The profile identifies the run models vulnerability on each prompt, which we call its vulnerability profile, is distinctive enough to identify its pretraining run. Earlier work identifies model from its behavior across versions and recovers the base model behind fine-tune (Pasquini et al., 2025; Foley et al., 2023). Here, many candidates share data recipe and differ only in their pretraining run. For each of the 75 runs, its model at post-training seed 1 serves as the reference and its model at seed 2 as the query. We assign each query to the reference whose profile correlates with its own most closely. The profiles cover 3,211 of the 3,212 adversarial-harmful prompts, leaving out the one prompt to which some model gave no coherent sample. This matching finds the right run for all 75 queries, against one in 75 for random guess. With 50 prompts drawn at random, the match finds the right run 98 % of the time on average over 200 random subsets (Figure 4b). Asked for the data recipe instead, the same matching gives much weaker signal. Each data recipes reference averages four models from two of its base models. Its queries are the models of the third base model, which the reference never saw, 50 queries in all. The match finds the right data recipe for 24 of the Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks 50 (48 %), against one in 25 for random guess. The data recipe reaches only about one in two with all 3,211 prompts, despite reference averaged over four models where runs reference is single model. We show this only across new post-training seed under one post-training recipe, not across different fine-tune. The prompts that break model are mark of its pretraining run far more than of its data recipe. 4. Related work Training randomness. Models differing only in training seed reach near-equal accuracy yet disagree on individual predictions (Zhong et al., 2021; DAmour et al., 2022) and generalize differently out of distribution (McCoy et al., 2020; Juneja et al., 2023). BERT encoder suites such as MultiBERTs nest seeds of task fine-tuning under pretraining seeds (Sellam et al., 2022). In these suites, new pretraining seed adds less disagreement on task predictions than new seed of task fine-tuning (Zhong et al., 2021). Measures of bias, however, shift with the pretraining seed (DAmour et al., 2022; Sellam et al., 2022). In decoder language models, PolyPythias varies this seed across many pretraining runs on one corpus and evaluates the base models (van der Wal et al., 2025), with analyses of such suites following how seeds diverge over training (Madaan et al., 2025; Fehlauer et al., 2025). None of these studies includes model trained to refuse. Variance of safety behavior. models aggregate harmfulness shifts with the seed of benign fine-tuning (Fraser et al., 2025), and sampling randomness flips its safety decision across sampling seeds and temperatures on about quarter of prompts, on average (Larsen, 2026). Prompts nonetheless rank alike in jailbreak diﬀiculty across attack runs on one model and across distinct models, though less so for one defended model (Hughes et al., 2025). Pretraining also matters: branches of one run differing only in final data refuse alike after SFT but differently after identical post-training (Lu et al., 2026). Outside safety, cognitive biases likewise follow the base model more than the instruction data (Itzhak et al., 2025). Telling the pretraining run apart from its data recipe takes two runs of one data recipe, which DataDecide (Magnusson et al., 2025) releases at 1B, given the same post-training. The refusal mechanism within and across models. Studies of refusal locate it in low-dimensional structure and find that structure in each model separately. In one account it is single direction in activation space (Arditi et al., 2024). Others describe cones of few dimensions (Wollschläger et al., 2025) or refusal signal encoded apart from harm (Zhao et al., 2025b). Work that stays inside one pretraining run follows this structure through posttraining stages (Labunets, 2026) and through pretraining checkpoints (Reblitz-Richardson, 2026). These works have not settled whether the structure exists before post-training (Arditi et al., 2024; Labunets, 2026; Reblitz-Richardson, 2026). Work that crosses distinct models carries refusal into other architectures by rotation (Bosco & Srinivasan, 2026) and between two model sizes by map (Oozeer et al., 2025). Across pretraining seeds rather than sizes, McCann (2026) compare features and steering vectors among nine Pythia70m base models, though not refusal. Refusal has thus been compared within one run or across models of different size, architecture or family (Reblitz-Richardson, 2026), never across runs of one data recipe. We make that comparison in Appendix F. Noise correction and fixed-seed reruns. Noise in two measures attenuates the correlation between them, and dividing by the square root of the product of their reliabilities recovers it (Spearman, 1904). Applied to models, the correction has been used to compare model with human ratings or brain recordings, with model reliability taken from readout heads retrained on one pretrained network (Depaolini & Hasson, 2026) or assumed perfect (Tan & Deng, 2026). Between two models, error consistency corrects only for chance agreement (Geirhos et al., 2020). second line of work finds that even runs with every seed fixed diverge in image classifiers and small or fine-tuned language models, through nondeterministic kernels or one tiny early perturbation (Summers & Dinneen, 2021; Zhuang et al., 2022; Bhojanapalli et al., 2021; Altıntaş et al., 2025). Neither line of work corrects comparison of two models for the noise of measuring each from sampled responses. 5. Discussion and limitations Two pretraining runs of the same data, given the same safety training, still break on noticeably different jailbreaks. Two models built on one base model correlate at 0.984 on average over data recipes. Two models built on different runs of the same data recipe correlate at only 0.811, close to the 0.779 of models trained on different data. This ordering appears in all 25 data recipes. The part of profile that differs between runs belongs to the pretraining run, and one checkpoint cannot show how large that part is. Our results indicate that jailbreak found on one checkpoint is evidence about one run, and only partly about the data behind it. This suggests that comparison of pretraining data and jailbreak evaluation each read better from more than one run. comparison of pretraining data usually asks only how often data recipes models break, and one model per data recipe answers even that question poorly. Compare two data recipes through one model each, and the ranking of the two by mean vulnerability is reversed in 23.4 % of comparisons, against the ranking from each data recipes six models taken 8 Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks together (Section 3.3). Such reversals come from how far single model can sit from its data recipes mean. On one model, data recipes mean vulnerability typically lies 3.44 points from its average over many models, on the judges scale. Three base models with one post-training seed each bring that distance down to 1.99 points. This suggests that three base models give clearer comparison of mean vulnerability on these data recipes than one model does. jailbreak evaluation reads the same checkpoint for different purpose, recording which attack template works best and which prompts break the model. Both answers move when the pretraining run changes. The best attack template survives new post-training seed in 67 % of pairs but new pretraining seed in only 27 %. Which prompts break checkpoint is also particular to its run. model from second post-training seed, matched by its vulnerability profile, picks out its own pretraining run among all 75 in 75 of 75 queries. random set of 50 prompts still finds the right run 98 % of the time (Section 3.3). Single prompts show the pattern too. prompt that breaks model at least nine times in ten does so on its MZ twin 75.0 % of the time but on another run of its data recipe only 60.9 %. This suggests that the attacks and prompts found on one checkpoint speak for its pretraining run and not only for its data. Our design has two limitations. The first is that every model comes from DataDecides family of pretraining runs and from the SFT and DPO stages of Tülu 3. Within that family we vary the corpus over 25 data recipes that differ in source, filtering and deduplication. The ancestry gaps interval over prompts excludes zero in every one, which suggests that the gap does not hinge on any single corpus. We also checked the safety data, and on one data recipe at 1B the gap reappears when second safety set replaces Tülu 3s safety set (Section 3.1, Appendix G). The second is that WildGuards refusal label, our primary judge, misses refusals on jailbreak prompts. It puts mean vulnerability at 0.528, and an audit of its labels adjusts it to 0.278 [0.230, 0.324] over audit items (Appendix D). Human labels on four models of one data recipe still give an uncorrected difference of 0.156 [0.036, 0.294] over prompts, an interval above zero (Section 3.1). Our largest models have 1B parameters, size set by what the comparison needs. It needs several full pretraining runs of one data recipe given the same post-training, and DataDecide releases three such runs for each data recipe at 1B. At larger sizes each run costs much more. Madaan et al. (2025) pretrained ten 7B runs that differed only in their initialization seed, and each took about 15,000 A100-hours. Short of that cost, the ancestry gap is positive on one data recipe at 150M, 300M and 1B (Section 3.1). Our released code and per-prompt judge labels facilitate future work that measures the ancestry gap in larger models.

sections.title: Impact statement
sections.content: We release our code on GitHub3 and the weights of the 150M, 300M and 1B models we post-trained, with their perprompt judge labels, on Hugging Face.4 The release leaves out the generated responses, and its judge labels name each prompt by id and source rather than by its text. Each prompt comes from published benchmark or dataset (Section 2), and we wrote no new jailbreak or harmful request. Our models are trained from public parts alone, DataDecides pretraining runs and data and Ai2s OLMo 2 post-training data, so anyone with the compute could train such models without our release. Jailbreak evaluations usually test one checkpoint, yet among our models jailbreak found to break one checkpoint may not break model from another pretraining run of the same data recipe (Section 3.1). new pretraining run of the same data may therefore need its own red-teaming, and where data recipe has several pretraining runs, red-teaming result may be better read across them than on one checkpoint (Section 5).
